checkpoints: Reach for `useSyncExternalStore` when the source of truth genuinely lives outside React — a browser API (window size) or a module-scope store shared by many readers.
It is the only primitive that guarantees every reader sees one consistent snapshot per frame under concurrent rendering: no tearing, no Provider needed.

The effect-mirror alternative (subscribing via `useEffect` then `setState`-ing the value into local state) is never a valid third option: it creates a redundant source of truth and updates only after commit.
Independent per-reader mirrors built this way can disagree with each other or simply freeze at their mount-time snapshot.

External state libraries are all built on top of this primitive because its contract — `subscribe` returns a cleanup, `getSnapshot` returns a stable reference, `Object.is` decides whether to re-render — is precisely the interface a store needs to expose.

Do NOT externalize state the React tree itself already owns: local form/UI state in `useState` keeps updates colocated and easy to test, and moving it out only adds subscription discipline while fixing no real consistency problem.
States the race's actual root cause: overlapping effect runs resolve in arrival order, not start order, so any correct fix must confirm a run is still the newest before letting it commit.
Frames `ignore` and `abort()` as two orthogonal guards solving different jobs, not two competing solutions to the same problem.

Defines `ignore` as a correctness guard: a boolean local to that specific effect run, flipped to `true` in the cleanup (which fires on the next `query` change or on unmount) and checked before a stale `.then` is allowed to write state.

Defines `abort()` as a separate efficiency guard: calling `controller.abort()` in that same cleanup cancels the in-flight request so the browser stops wasted work early, rather than preventing a stale write.

Explains why both are needed together: a stale response's `.then` callback can already be sitting in the microtask queue the instant before `abort()` runs, so it still executes to completion — only the `ignore` check stops it from committing.
Notes that `ignore` and the `AbortController` must be declared as locals inside the effect body for that run, not in a shared `useRef`, or a new run could silently reset the old run's guard.

Explains why raising the debounce delay is not a substitute for either guard: it only reduces how many requests fire, never guarantees the order they resolve in, so races can still occur on a slow or jittery network.

`filtered` is redundant derived state: it is fully computable from `query` via `filterUsers(USERS, query)`, yet it is stored as its own `useState` and synced with `useEffect([query])` — two sources of truth for the same information, and that is the root cause behind all 3 symptoms.

Symptom 1 (empty flash): `filtered` initializes to `[]`, and the effect only runs AFTER the first commit, so the first render paints an empty list even though an empty `query` should show all users right away.

Symptom 2 (render counter grows by 2 per keystroke): `setQuery` causes render #1 where `filtered` still holds the OLD query's result; React commits, then the effect runs and calls `setFiltered`, causing render #2.
Symptom 3 (previous query's matches shown for one frame): the frame between those two renders is exactly where `filtered` (the copy) lags behind `query` (the real source) before catching up.
The fix: delete the second `useState<User[]>` and the `useEffect` entirely, and compute `const filtered = filterUsers(USERS, query)` directly during render.
Only wrap it in `useMemo(() => filterUsers(USERS, query), [query])` if the filter were genuinely heavy, to cache it per dependency — still deriving in render, never an effect.

Verify by confirming the render counter grows by exactly 1 per keystroke, the first frame already shows all users, and the visible list always matches the current query in the same frame with no out-of-phase frame left.
The effect re-runs on every `query` change and fires one request per run.
It returns NO cleanup, so every old run's `.then` stays alive and commits the exact `query` its closure captured when that request fired.

With `re` ~340ms and `react` ~80ms, typing `re` then `react` means `react` commits FIRST, and the slower `re` response arrives later and overwrites state -- last-write-wins by arrival order, not by newest keyword.
Raising the debounce delay cannot fix this: debounce only lowers how many requests fire, and any two overlapping requests on a slow connection can still resolve out of order.
The fix lives inside the effect body: `let ignore = false` and `const controller = new AbortController()`, passing `controller.signal` into `searchApi`.

Guard the `.then` with `if (ignore) return` before committing, and return a cleanup doing `ignore = true` plus `controller.abort()` -- React runs this cleanup right before the next effect run and on unmount, marking the old run stale exactly as the new one begins.
The `.catch` should swallow only `AbortError` (expected) and let real errors surface, not swallow everything.
Regression test: script the slow-then-fast sequence, wait past the slow request's ~340ms window, and assert `committedQuery === "react"` with exactly one aborted request counted.

Most severe: `getSnapshot` builds a new object literal on every call, and since React compares old vs new snapshot with `Object.is`, two different literals never share identity so `Object.is` is always `false`.
This makes React believe the store just changed on EVERY check, causing an infinite re-render loop plus the "getSnapshot should be cached" warning.
Fix: cache the object and only build a new one when `width`/`height` actually change, or return a primitive value instead.

Moderately severe: `subscribe` is declared inside the hook body so its reference changes every render, making React detach-then-reattach the resize listener repeatedly even though the logic never actually changed -- wasted churn, not a data-correctness bug like the first one.
Fix: hoist `subscribe` to module scope or wrap it in `useCallback`.
Least severe but still merge-blocking for an SSR app: the hook has no `getServerSnapshot`, so server rendering (no `window`) throws or produces a server/client hydration mismatch.
Fix: always supply a `getServerSnapshot` returning a safe default like `{ width: 0, height: 0 }`.

Verify: the cache warning is gone and the render counter stays flat across parent re-renders; `addEventListener`/`removeEventListener` counts stay flat across re-renders; an SSR pass confirms `getServerSnapshot` is actually called and doesn't throw.
Polling is the request/response model: the client must actively ask, so latency always equals the poll interval.
Every polling round pays the full HTTP header cost whether or not there is anything new.
Realtime needs the opposite: the server actively PUSHES events over a durable full-duplex channel.

That channel is opened exactly ONCE via an HTTP Upgrade handshake, after which both sides push frames to each other instantly with no new request needed -- that is exactly what a WebSocket-style connection is.
In exchange you get millisecond-level latency and a header cost paid only once at handshake.
The tradeoff: you must manage reconnects, a ping/pong heartbeat, and horizontal scaling of connection state across nodes yourself -- realtime is not free.
Polling faster (shrinking the interval from 2 seconds to 200ms) never fixes the root problem -- it only trades latency for system load.
The flaw is in the communication MODEL itself, not the polling frequency.

A DB boolean models presence as durable data -- something written down that stays until overwritten -- but presence only exists as long as connections exist, so the state has to be DERIVED at each moment, not stored as a fixed record.

The problem shows up clearly once a user holds multiple connections at once (several tabs/devices): a single `true/false` flag gets overwritten to `false` when one tab closes, flipping the user offline even though another tab is still open.
The flag has no room to distinguish "closed one tab" from "fully offline", because it only carries one bit of information while reality is a count of live connections.
The correct model keeps, per user, a SET of live connection ids; "online" is defined as that set being non-empty.
Every new connection adds its id to the set; every connection that closes removes its id.

Only two transitions are worth broadcasting: the set going from empty to non-empty (user just came online) and the set going back to empty (user is now truly offline) -- so opening/closing one of several tabs never produces a false notification.

Cleanup can't be optional: the server must proactively remove a connection's id from the set inside its own disconnect handler, since the client can never be trusted to announce it's leaving (network drops, a tab can be killed abruptly with no chance to send an "I'm leaving" signal).

Residual gap: if the server process crashes before the disconnect handler runs, the id stays stuck in the set forever ("ghost presence"), which is why production adds a heartbeat plus a TTL so stale entries expire even when no disconnect event ever fires.

Clients should only ever see a chat message once it has actually been committed to the database; broadcasting the payload before the save completes inverts that invariant and is a defect in the fundamental design, not a minor style issue.

When the broadcast fires immediately and the subsequent `saveMessage(...)` call then rejects — a constraint violation, the database being down — no row is ever written, so a page refresh or a replay-on-join read from `chat_message` shows nothing: every client in the room just watched a message that literally never existed.

Calling `saveMessage(...)` without `await` turns its returned promise into an unobserved floating promise; a rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection that stays invisible unless it eventually crashes the process, instead of surfacing anywhere the caller can react to it.

Building the broadcast payload from the raw incoming `body` instead of the row returned by the save means it can never carry the database-assigned monotonic `id` or `createdAt`, so there is no stable key for ordering concurrent sends or for a later replay/pagination by id.

The disciplined fix is to `await` `saveMessage(...)` first, construct the broadcast payload from the committed row's fields (`id`, `senderId`, `nickname`, `room`, `text`, `createdAt`), and let a rejected save throw (e.g. a `WsException`) so the sender's ack surfaces the error and the room sees nothing for a message that doesn't exist.

Saving before broadcasting adds the write's latency in front of fanout instead of after it, but that cost is worth paying because correctness — never showing a phantom message that isn't backed by a row — matters more than shaving milliseconds off perceived responsiveness.

If asynchronous retry is genuinely required for throughput, the correct production pattern is an outbox table or an external queue that feeds the broadcast only after the write is durable, never emitting optimistically before the row exists.

A failure-injection test that forces `saveMessage` to reject should assert that zero sockets received a broadcast and that the sender's ack carries an error, paired with a happy-path test asserting the broadcast payload's `id` matches the database-assigned value on the persisted row.

Event volume in a typing indicator scales multiplicatively: keystrokes-per-second per typist × (room size − 1) receivers × number of concurrent typists, so a 60-WPM typist alone produces roughly 5 emits/sec that fan out to ~199 sockets in a 200-member room — on the order of a thousand frames per second from one person.

Neither the client's per-keystroke `socket.emit("typing", ...)` nor the gateway's unconditional `client.to(roomId).emit(...)` relay is functionally broken; the cost comes from tying emit frequency to keystroke rate rather than to the signal's real granularity.

A typing indicator is an ephemeral, lossy-tolerant signal: the receiver already fades it on its own after a fixed window (~1.5s) with no new event, so its true resolution is 'once per fade window', not 'once per keystroke' — any emit faster than that renews an indicator that was never going to expire and is pure waste.

The correct fix sits on the client, at the emit source, because that's the cheapest point to cut volume before it reaches the socket or the server's fan-out at all — fixing it downstream (in the gateway relay) still pays the full network cost of every keystroke reaching the server.

A leading-edge throttle keyed to the fade window is the mechanism: emit immediately on the first keystroke of a burst, then suppress further emits until the fade duration has elapsed, so one emit sustains the receiver's indicator for the whole burst instead of one emit per keystroke.

This change preserves UX exactly: since the receiver's fade timer resets on any emit received within its window, a coarser emit schedule produces the identical appear-then-fade behavior as the fine-grained one, just with an order of magnitude less traffic.
Typing state should remain unpersisted — it has no value as durable data, so there is no persistence trade-off to reconsider here, only the emit-frequency problem.

A per-connection server-side rate limit (e.g., a token bucket keyed by client id) on the gateway is a defense-in-depth backstop, not the primary fix — it protects against a legacy client or bug that bypasses the client-side throttle, but it isn't where the real savings come from.

Verification requires two separate checks: a load test measuring relayed typing frames/sec before and after under simulated multi-typist load to confirm an order-of-magnitude drop, and a two-client UX test confirming the indicator still appears promptly on the first keystroke and fades roughly 1.5s after the last one.

The `append` method assigns a monotonic per-room sequence number but never trims the room's history array, so each room's in-memory array grows without bound for the entire lifetime of the process — a steady, unrecoverable memory climb.

The `replaySince` method filters messages newer than `lastSeq` but places no limit on how many it returns, so a client that has been offline for hours gets every missed message in a single payload — a multi-second freeze on the client and a giant frame on the wire.

The unbounded write side and the unbounded read side are the same underlying bug viewed from opposite ends of one log: no eviction on write produces the memory climb, and no cap on read produces the oversized reconnect payload.

Fixing only one end is insufficient defence-in-depth: capping the array at append (a ring buffer that evicts the oldest entry via `shift()` once past a size cap) bounds server memory, while capping the filtered result in `replaySince` (e.g. with `.slice()`) bounds the client's payload regardless of how long it was offline — both are needed simultaneously.

Bounding the ring buffer has an honest cost: once a client's `lastSeq` falls further back than the buffer's retained window, the server can no longer reconstruct the full gap from memory alone, and those older messages are permanently unrecoverable from the in-memory log.

Once history must survive beyond the ring buffer's horizon, it belongs in durable storage such as Postgres, with the existing monotonic `seq` reused as a pagination cursor for a 'load older' fetch, while the in-memory ring buffer is kept only as a fast cache of recent history.

The size of the ring-buffer/replay cap should be derived from real traffic numbers — a room's message rate multiplied by the offline duration the system wants to tolerate — rather than picked arbitrarily.

Correct behavior for both bounds should be verified concretely: a soak or load test confirming per-room memory plateaus once the cap is reached, and a long-offline reconnect test confirming the replay ack's item count never exceeds the cap while still containing the newest messages.
